concept.body: Applied height problems: (1) draw the right triangle; (2) mark the horizontal and the given angle; (3) assign roles — vertical height and ground distance are legs, sight lines and strings are hypotenuses; (4) pick the ratio joining your known and unknown; (5) add eye height if the instrument reads from eye level.

explanationVariants: The 20 m ladder is the hypotenuse; height is opposite 70°: 20·sin 70° ≈ 18.79 m.
SOH with the ladder as hypotenuse: 20 × 0.9397 ≈ 18.79 m.

widget.prompt: A 20 m ladder leans at 70° to the ground. How high up the wall does it reach (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 6.84 = 20·cos 70° is the FOOT's distance from the wall. Height is opposite the angle: 20·sin 70° ≈ 18.79.
54.95 = 20·tan 70° uses tangent — but 20 m is the ladder, the HYPOTENUSE. Sine: ≈ 18.79.

steps.body: Trig turns one angle and one distance into heights no tape measure reaches. The routine: sketch the right triangle, mark the horizontal, place the angle, label each side's role FROM that angle — then it's Chapter 3. One wrinkle: instruments sit at eye level, so add the observer's **eye height** to the triangle's answer.

widget.prompt: You stand 40 m from a building; your clinometer (at eye level, 1.6 m up) reads 55° to the roof. The value 40·tan 55° gives which height?

options.label: The roof's height ABOVE YOUR EYE — add 1.6 m for the full building
options.feedback: The triangle starts at eye level, so its vertical leg misses the bottom 1.6 m. Total ≈ 57.13 + 1.6 = 58.73 m.

options.label: The full height of the building
options.feedback: The triangle's base is your EYE, 1.6 m off the ground — its vertical leg stops short. Add 1.6 m: ≈ 58.73 m.

options.label: The length of your line of sight
options.feedback: The line of sight is the hypotenuse (40 ÷ cos 55°). 40·tan 55° is the vertical LEG — height above the eye.

options.label: The height minus the 40 m distance
options.feedback: Horizontal distance is never subtracted from height — they're perpendicular legs. 40·tan 55° IS the height above eye level.

explanationVariants: 40·tan 55° ≈ 57.13 m above the eye, plus 1.6 m of eye height: ≈ 58.73 m.

widget.prompt: Same setup: 40 m away, 55° elevation from an eye height of 1.6 m. Total building height in meters (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 57.13 = 40·tan 55° stops at eye level — the bottom 1.6 m is missing. Total ≈ 58.73.
34.37 = 40·sin 55° + 1.6 treats the 40 m ground distance as the line of sight. It's the adjacent LEG: 40·tan 55° + 1.6 ≈ 58.73.

steps.body: Not every problem is leg-and-leg. A kite string, a ladder, a zip line — those ARE the hypotenuse. String 90 m at 48° elevation: the kite's height is opposite, the string is the hypotenuse, so **sine**: 90·sin 48° ≈ 66.88 m. Read the story to learn which side each length plays.

explanationVariants: The 90 m string is the hypotenuse; height is opposite 48°: 90·sin 48° ≈ 66.88 m.

widget.prompt: A kite flies on a taut 90 m string at 48° elevation. How high is the kite (2 decimals)? Ignore the flyer's height.

commonErrors.feedback: 60.22 = 90·cos 48° is the HORIZONTAL distance to below the kite. Height is the opposite leg: 90·sin 48° ≈ 66.88.
99.96 = 90·tan 48° uses tangent — but the 90 m string is the HYPOTENUSE, which tangent never touches. Sine: ≈ 66.88.

steps.body: Sanity checks belong in every applied answer. A height can't exceed the hypotenuse (a kite can't fly higher than its string is long). Small angles mean LONG horizontal reach and small height; steep angles the reverse. If a 12° depression yields a horizontal distance SHORTER than the height, an operation got flipped.

widget.prompt: Both kites fly on 90 m of string. Read opp/hyp at the starting 30°, then drag to 60°. If doubling the angle doubled the height, opp/hyp would have to double too.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle a couple of times first. Both kites are on the SAME 90 m string, so before comparing angles it is worth seeing that the string length is not what the ratio is tracking.
widget.successFeedback: 60°, and opp/hyp reads 0.866 — not 1.000. Doubling the angle did not double the height: on 90 m of string, 45 m became 77.9 m, a factor of 1.73. Height follows the sine of the angle, and sine does not grow in step with the angle it is handed.
widget.lowFeedback: opp/hyp is under 0.866, so this kite is flying lower than the 60° one you are after. Open the angle.
widget.highFeedback: opp/hyp is above 0.866 — past 60°, steeper than the second kite's string. Close the angle back toward it.

predict.prompt: Two kites, both on 90 m of string, one at 30° and one at 60°. The 60° kite's height will be…

options.label: More than the 30° kite's, but less than double it

predict.reveal: Higher, but not double: 45 m becomes 77.9 m, a factor of about 1.73. Doubling the ANGLE is not doubling the height, because the height is 90·sin θ and sine bends — it climbs fastest near 0° and flattens as it approaches 90°.

explanationVariants: The altitude (2500 m) is opposite the relocated 12°; the ground distance is adjacent — tangent, with x on the bottom.

widget.prompt: A plane at 2500 m altitude sights an airport at 12° depression. Which computation gives the horizontal GROUND distance?

options.label: 2500 ÷ tan 12°
options.feedback: Relocated angle at the airport: tan 12° = 2500/x → x = 2500 ÷ tan 12° ≈ 11,761.58 m.

options.label: 2500 × tan 12°
options.feedback: Multiplying gives ≈ 531 m — a shallow 12° glide can't reach the ground that fast. x is on the BOTTOM: divide.

options.label: 2500 ÷ sin 12°
options.feedback: That's the slant LINE-OF-SIGHT (≈ 12,024 m), the hypotenuse — not the ground leg. Use tangent: 2500 ÷ tan 12°.

options.label: 2500 × cos 12°
options.feedback: Cosine needs the hypotenuse, but 2500 is the vertical LEG. Leg-to-leg is tangent: 2500 ÷ tan 12°.

hints: Relocate 12° to the airport; the 2500 m altitude is opposite it, the ground distance x adjacent.
tan 12° = 2500/x — the unknown is on the bottom.
explanationVariants: x = 2500 ÷ tan 12° ≈ 11,761.58 m — far longer than the altitude, as a shallow angle demands.
Dividing the altitude by tan 12° gives ≈ 11,761.58 m of ground distance.

widget.prompt: Compute it: the plane is at 2500 m, depression to the airport 12°. Horizontal ground distance in meters (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 531.39 = 2500·tan 12° multiplies — and fails the sanity check: a 12° glide is SHALLOW, so the reach must dwarf the height. Divide: ≈ 11,761.58.
12,024.34 = 2500 ÷ sin 12° is the slant distance the plane actually flies — the hypotenuse, not the ground leg: ≈ 11,761.58.

takeaways: Sketch, mark the horizontal, label sides FROM the angle — then it's ordinary solving.
Instruments read from eye level: add eye height for total height.
Strings, ladders, and sight lines are hypotenuses (sine/cosine); ground-and-height pairs are legs (tangent).
